c) Plot an examine the main featuers of the graph, checking in particular whether there is 
i. A trend, ii. A seasonal component, iii. Any apparent sharp changes in behavior. 

```{r data}
data(discoveries)
x <- discoveries
t <- time(x)

start(x); end(x); frequency(x); length(x)
summary(x)
c(mean = mean(x), variance = var(x), sd = sd(x))
```
Plotting and Examining the main features- time plot

```{r timeplot}
plot(x, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.6,
     main = "Great Inventions and Scientific Discoveries, 1860-1959",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Number of discoveries")
abline(h = mean(x), lty = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", legend = "Overall mean", lty = 2, col = "red", bty = "n")
```

Trend
```{r trend-tests}
# Linear regression on time
fit_lm <- lm(x ~ t)
summary(fit_lm)

t <- time(discoveries)
plot(discoveries, main = "Trend check", ylab = "Number of discoveries")
lines(lowess(t, discoveries), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(lm(discoveries ~ t), col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)

summary(lm(discoveries ~ t))
```
-There is a weak, slowly varying/ mild downward linear trend, not a clear one 
-This is a reason to check stationarity formally


Seasonality: 
The data are annual (frequency = 1), so there is no seasonal component. A periodogram checks for any longer cycle.

```{r seasonal}
frequency(discoveries)
spec.pgram(discoveries, taper = 0, log = "no", main = "Periodogram")
```
- There is no seasonal component (the data are annual with frequency = 1, so there is no within-year period to repeat)

Sharp Changes:
```{r changes}
# mean and variance in four 25-year blocks
block <- rep(1:4, each = 25)
tapply(discoveries, block, mean)
tapply(discoveries, block, var)

boxplot(as.numeric(discoveries) ~ block, names = c("1860-84", "1885-09", "1910-34", "1935-59"),
        main = "Counts by 25-year block")
```


- There are no abrupt structural breaks, but there are a few notable occurences:
The series reachest its maximum of 12 in 1885, and counts of 10 and 9 follow around 1887 hich is the most extreme stretch and produces the large residual in the regression
-There are changes in levels across blocks (block means are 2.68, 4.20, 3.72, and 1.80)
- There is a change in variance (block variance are 3.23, 8.25, 4.29, and 1.58, so variability moves with the level)
There is no single sharp break, but there is a gradual shift in mean and variance with a burst in high values in the 1880s.
0s and quieter lower periods after about 1935. Since the variance rises and falls with the mean, the series is not strictly stationary in variance as it stands. 


d. Transformation and stationarity

```{r transform}
library(tseries)
data(discoveries)
x <- discoveries

y <- sqrt(x + 3/8)

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(x, main = "Original", ylab = "Count")
plot(y, main = "Square-root transform", ylab = "sqrt(count + 3/8)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Does the transform stabilize the variance across blocks? 
```{r variance-check}
block <- rep(1:4, each = 25)
rbind(original = tapply(x, block, var),
      sqrt     = tapply(y, block, var))
```

Stationarity tests on the transformed series
```{r tests}
adf.test(y)    # H0: non-stationary (unit root)
kpss.test(y)   # H0: stationary
```

Check whether differencing (lag 1) is needed or harmful
```{r diff}
d1 <- diff(y, lag = 1)
plot(d1, main = "Lag-1 difference of sqrt series")
adf.test(d1)
c(var_y = var(y), var_d1 = var(d1))
acf(d1, main = "ACF of differenced series")
```

I applied a square-root transformation to stabilize the variance because the data are counts. The ADF test (p = 0.027) and KPSS test (p = 0.055) suggest the transformed series is stationary. Differencing increased the variance and produced a lag-1 ACF near −0.5, suggesting over-differencing. Therefore, I will model the transformed series without differencing (d=0).

e. 
ACF and PACF

```{r acf-pacf}
y <- sqrt(discoveries + 3/8)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(y, lag.max = 20, main = "Sample ACF of sqrt series")
pacf(y, lag.max = 20, main = "Sample PACF of sqrt series")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


Fitting the candidate models suggested by the plots
```{r fit}
m_ar1   <- arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0))
m_ar2   <- arima(y, order = c(2, 0, 0))
m_ma1   <- arima(y, order = c(0, 0, 1))
m_arma  <- arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 1))

m_ar2
c(AR1 = AIC(m_ar1), AR2 = AIC(m_ar2), MA1 = AIC(m_ma1), ARMA11 = AIC(m_arma))
```

Theoretical ACF/PACF using the fitted coefficients
```{r theoretical}
lags <- 1:20
phi1 <- coef(m_ar1)["ar1"]
phi2 <- coef(m_ar2)[c("ar1", "ar2")]

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lags, ARMAacf(ar = phi1, lag.max = 20)[-1], type = "h",
     main = "Theoretical ACF: AR(1)", ylab = "ACF"); abline(h = 0)
plot(lags, ARMAacf(ar = phi1, lag.max = 20, pacf = TRUE), type = "h",
     main = "Theoretical PACF: AR(1)", ylab = "PACF"); abline(h = 0)
plot(lags, ARMAacf(ar = phi2, lag.max = 20)[-1], type = "h",
     main = "Theoretical ACF: AR(2)", ylab = "ACF"); abline(h = 0)
plot(lags, ARMAacf(ar = phi2, lag.max = 20, pacf = TRUE), type = "h",
     main = "Theoretical PACF: AR(2)", ylab = "PACF"); abline(h = 0)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The ACF tails off after lags 1 and 2, while the PACF cuts off after lag 2, suggesting an AR(2) model. However, ARMA(1,1) has a slightly lower AIC (178.67 vs. 178.77), so I will choose ARMA(1,1) as my preliminary model. Since the AIC values are nearly identical, I will compare residual diagnostics to determine whether it fits the data adequately.
